deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page). X is a topological space and F is a family of subsets of X satisfying axioms a)–f). G_F is the sheaf of subsets that are locally in F: a set A ⊂ U is a section over U if every x in U has a neighbourhood V_x and some B_x in F with A∩V_x = B_x∩V_x. Write F̄_U = Γ(U, G_F) and F̄ = F̄_X. Grothendieck tests the case F = C_P, the family of unions of cells (here called 'feuilles' X_i) of a cellular decomposition or stratification P of X. He asks when F̄_U = F_U for every open U that lies in F. The previous page showed this forces all cells to be connected. This page proves the converse.

(1) Reduction to U = X. Let A be locally a union of leaves. It suffices to show that every leaf X_i meeting A lies inside A. Near any point x, A∩V = B∩V with B a union of leaves. So A∩X_i∩V is either X_i∩V or empty. Hence A∩X_i is open and closed in X_i. Since X_i is connected and A∩X_i is nonempty, X_i ⊂ A. Conclusion: for a decomposition with connected cells, 'locally a union of cells' equals 'a union of cells', so F̄ = F. Applying this to U in F gives F̄_U = F_U.

(2) Arbitrary open U. The same argument shows that for any open U and any A in F̄_U, each A∩X_i is clopen in X_i∩U. So A is a union of connected components of the sets X_i∩U.

(3) The converse fails. Grothendieck asks whether every union of such components lies in F̄_U, in particular a single component.
- First example: X = U = ℝ with strata X_0 = {0} and X_1 = ℝ* (struck draft: F = {∅, ℝ, {0}, ℝ*}). Then ℝ+ is a component of X_1 but is not locally a union of strata at 0, so ℝ+ is not in F̄.
- Second example, with connected strata and U ≠ X: X is the one-point compactification of ℝ, i.e. the circle S¹. Take X_0 = {0}, X_1 = X − {0} ≅ ℝ (connected), and U = ℝ = X − {∞}. Then X_1∩U = ℝ* is disconnected, and the same failure occurs.

Purpose. The notes probe how the 'locally-F' sheaf behaves under restriction to opens that are not in F. This is the theme of the next page: condition f) is stable under restriction to opens in F but not to arbitrary opens. It is part of Grothendieck's 1974 attempt to axiomatize 'tame' (modérée) families of subsets.
errors: The text says X_i ∩ A is 'à la fois ouverte et fermée de A'; what the argument needs, and actually shows, is that it is clopen in X_i. This is a slip of the pen.

In the second example the deleted point should be a finite point (0), not ∞, for U = ℝ = X − {∞} to give a counterexample. Grothendieck writes X_0 = {0}, which is correct. One just has to read X̂ = ℝ ∪ {∞} with 0 ∈ ℝ.

ideas.what: For a decomposition into connected cells, a set that is locally a union of cells is globally a union of cells; the clopen-intersection argument
ideas.modern_name: Elementary property of stratifications/partitions with connected strata

ideas.what: The sheaf of 'locally-F' subsets does not commute with restriction to arbitrary (non-F) opens; counterexample ℝ with strata {0} and ℝ*, and its circle variant with connected strata
ideas.modern_name: Need for a restricted topology / site of admissible (definable) opens in tame geometry
ideas.usually_credited_to: Delfs–Knebusch (semialgebraic spaces, restricted topology, early 1980s); o-minimal sites (later work, e.g. Edmundo et al.)
ideas.where_published: Tame topology is only programmatically discussed in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), §5; this detail is not there

deep.surprise_reason: These are correct but elementary point-set arguments about stratifications with connected strata, plus a standard counterexample. The only modern resonance is that tame structures behave well only on 'admissible' opens. That is now standard via Delfs–Knebusch restricted topologies and o-minimal sites, and the page does not go beyond noticing the failure.
transcription_corrections: The image indeed reads 'ouverte et fermée de A' (Grothendieck's slip); the transcription is faithful but the mathematics requires 'de X_i'.

The struck-out formula in the example reads approximately '\overline{F} = \{\emptyset, \mathbb{R}, \{0\}, \mathbb{R}^*\}' (that is, the family F = C_P itself); this reading is consistent with the image.
'X = \hat{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{S}^1' is plausible (one-point compactification of ℝ); the superscript is hard to read, but the circle is clearly meant.
